newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway's Aker in surprise merger with RGI.
newsitem.headline: Norway's Aker in surprise merger with RGI.

text.p: Norwegian engineering and offshore group Aker ASA and investment group Resource Group International ASA (RGI) announced a merger on Tuesday just one day after declaring talks had been discontinued.

The combined company, Aker RGI ASA, will be one of the largest industrial groups in Scandinavia with annual revenues of 19 billion crowns ($2.93 billion) and a market capitalisation of nine billion crowns. The deal values one Aker share at 2.15 RGI shares.

The company will focus on three core areas -- seafood, cement and oil and gas -- but will look for other areas to stretch its newly-found financial muscle, said Bjoern Rune Gjelsten, Aker chairman and chairman designated of the new joint board.
"By merging we will create a powerful Norwegian-based industrial owner. Aker RGI will have substantial investment capacity, both in the Nordic region and on a European scale.
"That will be used to pursue further expansion and value growth to the benefit of both shareholders and employers," Gjelsten told a news conference.
Gjelsten is co-owner of RGI with charismatic entrepreneur Kjell Inge Roekke, who will have a shareholding in the new company of 33 percent.
Gjelsten said the surprise announcement, which followed the breakdown of negotiations at the weekend, was a result of the enthusiasm shown by both companies for a merger.

"What truly brought us back together was the real will on both sides to go through with the merger. The more we worked on it the more it became clear that it is right for the parties involved and the new group."
The proposed merger, subject to formal approval by shareholders next month, will bring together one of Norway's oldest companies with a newcomer on the corporate scene.
Aker was founded in 1841 while RGI, which has quickly become the world's largest white fish fishing and processing operation, was listed on the Oslo Bourse little more than two months ago.

RGI's other interests include sports goods and outdoor apparel, shipbuilding, real estate, packaging office supplies and finance. Currently registered in the Netherlands Antilles, it will transfer operations to Norway under the merger plan.
Analysts, caught offguard by the deal, remained unsure of the proposal.

"What strikes you first looking at the combined group is that these are not overlapping businesses. Fish and concrete and oil and gas don't match at least not in terms of synergy," said an Oslo-based analyst.

Aker has recently transformed itself into an industrial group, first by separating its cement and building group in 1995 and joining forces with Sweden's Skanska AB to form the Nordic cement group Scancem.
Last month shareholders approved a merger of Aker's Oil and Gas Technology division and offshore supplier Maritime Group to form Aker Maritime ASA.
Aker's share price was trading 2.50 crowns down by mid session at 130 crowns while RGI had lost five crowns at 61. ($1=6.496 Norwegian Crown)
